item.title: Obituaries for September 11
item.description:
Blanche Dora Freitas Angay, 77, of Mountain View died Aug. 24 at Hilo Benioff Medical Center. Born in Ka‘u, she was a retired public school cafeteria worker. Visitation 4-6 p.m. Wednesday (Sep. 16) at Dodo Mortuary Chapel. Service at 6 p.m. Visitation again 9 a.m.-10:30 a.m. at the mortuary. Service at 10:30 a.m. Burial noon at Homelani Memorial Park. Survived by son, Steven (Melissa) Angay Jr. of Lexington Park, Md.; brother, Roy P. Freitas of Maui; sisters, Rosemarie Freitas Angay of Kona and Bernadette Dianne Freitas Kawailima of Keaukaha; three grandchildren; aunts, uncles, cousins, nieces, and nephews. Arrangements by Dodo Mortuary.

The post Obituaries for September 11 appeared first on Hawaii Tribune-Herald.

item.title: For a photographer, the towers were an ever-present focal point
item.description:
Keith Meyers joined The New York Times as a staff photographer in 1980. Fascinated by the World Trade Center, he often made the towers part of his photographs. After the 9/11 terrorist attack, he photographed the towers for the final time, making aerial images from ground zero that became part of the Times’ team of photographers’ Pulitzer Prize-winning news photography coverage.

The post For a photographer, the towers were an ever-present focal point appeared first on Hawaii Tribune-Herald.

item.title: Obituaries for September 10
item.description:
Conrad Byron Alicuben, 89, of Hilo died Aug. 8 at Yukio Okutsu State Veterans Home. Born in Hilo, he was a retired electrical inspector supervisor for the county, the former Sheraton Waiakea Village and the former Hilo Coast Processing Co., and U.S. Air Force veteran. Visitation 4-5 p.m. Monday (Sep. 14) at Dodo Mortuary Chapel. Memorial service at 5 p.m. Private family committal service with military honors Tuesday (Sep. 15) at East Hawaii Veterans Cemetery No. 2 Pavilion. Survived by wife, Peggy Alicuben of Hilo; son, Conrad “Cy” Alicuben of Hilo; daughter, Cristy (Ethan) Castillo of Hilo; hanai son, Nikolas (Nicole) Geraci of Hilo; brother, Donald (Mae) Alicuben of Hilo; sisters-in-law, Jean Haraga of Kaneohe, Oahu, and Janet Ichinose of Hilo; brothers-in-law, Gary (Alice) Ichinose of Hilo and Roy (Sandi) Ichinose of Pearl City, Oahu; five grandchildren and two great-grandchildren; nieces and nephews. Arrangements by Dodo Mortuary.

The post Obituaries for September 10 appeared first on Hawaii Tribune-Herald.

item.title: Dept. of Education kicks off 2026 sports program
item.description:
Source: ASG media release

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — Last Friday morning joy and enthusiasm filled the American Samoa Department of Education main office in Utulei as leaders, educators, and families gathered to celebrate the official opening of the 2026 academic sports year. Acting Governor Pulumataala Ae Ae Jr. joined the government leaders, Department of Education leadership, high school administrators, coaches, community partners, parents, and student athletes. 

Principal Leo'o Dr. Patrick Danielson served as master of ceremonies, welcoming all guests and introducing Stake President Lotoa Lotoa Jr., who offered opening words of encouragement and led the invocation to set a positive tone for the event. In his special remarks, Acting Governor Pulumataala expressed immense gratitude for the continuation of student sports programs. Recalling a visit to Afono Elementary School's new gymnasium, where he noticed a lack of sports equipment and later returned to donate essential items, he reaffirmed his dedication to finding resources and funding for ASDOE athletics. He urged student athletes to strive for excellence in both academics and sports, while encouraging them to make healthy choices that support a long and fulfilling life. 

ASDOE Director Maefau Dr. Mary Taufete'e expressed her sincere appreciation to all community partners, departments, and sports associations that joined forces with the department. Emphasizing the power of collaboration, she noted that building a strong network of support, much like a house supported by many posts, ensures a brighter future for the territory's youth. The program reached an exciting highlight with the ceremonial first throw. Acting Governor Pulumataala threw the first football to a student athlete of Tafuna High School, followed by Director Taufete'e alongside House representatives and community partners, threw sports balls to student team captains from all of the high schools to officially kick off the season. 

Principal Leo'o Dr. Patrick Danielson delivered closing remarks on behalf of the Director and the Department of Education, expressing gratitude to the attendees for their presence in celebrating this significant occasion. Representative Faimealelei Allen took to the podium to offer remarks of appreciation, wishing ASDOE and its student athletes a successful year while pledging ongoing support from the legislature. The memorable gathering concluded with a closing prayer led by Stake President Lotoa Lotoa Jr.

 

Section: 
Local News
Tags: 
2026 academic sports year

item.title: Obituaries for September 9
item.description:
Conrad Byron Alicuben, 89, of Hilo died Aug. 8 at Yukio Okutsu State Veterans Home. Born in Hilo, he was a retired electrical inspector supervisor for the county, the former Sheraton Waiakea Village and the former Hilo Coast Processing Co., and U.S. Air Force veteran. Visitation 4-5 p.m. Monday (Sep. 14) at Dodo Mortuary Chapel. Memorial service at 5 p.m. Private family committal service with military honors Tuesday (Sep. 15) at East Hawaii Veterans Cemetery No. 2 Pavilion. Survived by son, Conrad “Cy” Alicuben of Hilo; daughter, Cristy (Ethan) Castillo of Hilo; hanai son, Nikolas (Nicole) Geraci of Hilo; brother, Donald (Mae) Alicuben of Hilo; sisters-in-law, Jean Haraga of Kaneohe, Oahu, and Janet Ichinose of Hilo; brothers-in-law, Gary (Alice) Ichinose of Hilo and Roy (Sandi) Ichinose of Pearl City, Oahu; five grandchildren and two great-grandchildren; nieces and nephews. Arrangements by Dodo Mortuary.

The post Obituaries for September 9 appeared first on Hawaii Tribune-Herald.

item.title: Alaska Court of Appeals dismisses voter misconduct indictment against Am Samoan woman
item.description:
By 
Right to Democracy staff

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — The Alaska Court of Appeals, in a unanimous opinion, has ruled against the State of Alaska in its criminal prosecution of Tupe Smith, an American Samoan woman living in Whittier who had been instructed by local officials to mark she was a “U.S. citizen” on voter registration forms after she told them she was a “U.S. national.” 

The Court ruled that to prove voter misconduct the state must establish “that the defendant acted with a consciousness of wrongdoing in purposely or deliberately making a false sworn statement under an oath.” The decision reversed an earlier ruling by the Alaska Superior Court.

“The state’s prosecution against me and my family has been extremely difficult. I feel vindicated by today’s court decision. But at the same time I worry it will not mean the end of the state’s criminal targeting of the American Samoan community in Whittier,” said Tupe Smith, who the State arrested on charges of voter misconduct shortly after she was elected to serve on her local school board in 2023. 

The Court ruled that “Smith would not be criminally liable if she did not realize that checking the U.S. citizen box was wrong,” explaining that “she stated that she had been told by Whittier election officials that if there was not a box to check for U.S. national, she should check the box for U.S. citizen.” The Court further noted that when the police interviewed her “she was confused about her status and her eligibility to vote,” with the court observing that “Alaska law sometimes expressly treats U.S. nationals as U.S. citizens.” 

“We appreciate the Court’s thoughtful ruling, which in addition to following the law just makes common sense,” said Neil Weare, Co-Director of Right to Democracy, who represents Ms. Smith along with her husband Michael Pese, who is also facing prosecution. “Being confused about what box to check, especially after public officials tell you to check a certain box, should not be considered a crime at all, much less a felony that could mean up to five years in jail.”

“We are delighted for Ms. Smith, whose case has always centered on a simple principle: people should not face felony charges for voter misconduct absent proof that they intended to do something wrong. The Alaska Court of Appeals’ opinion faithfully applies the law and provides important guidance on how Alaska’s voter-misconduct statute should be understood in future cases,” said Whitney Brown, a partner at Stoel Rives, who argued the case before the Alaska Court of Appeals on behalf of Ms. Smith.

“The state should take this moment to pause and reconsider its criminal prosecution of American Samoans in Whittier. Not just of Ms. Smith, but her husband Michael Pese and all the others it has charged,” said Charles Ala’ilima, an American Samoan attorney who also represents Ms. Smith and Mr. Pese. “American Samoa’s Governor, Congresswoman, and legislative leaders have all expressed concerns about Alaska’s ongoing criminal prosecutions of our people, and we hope Alaska prosecutors will take that into consideration as they plan their next steps.” 

If the state chooses not to bring its criminal prosecution to an end, it has a few options. The State could appeal the decision to the Alaska Supreme Court. Or it could re-indict Ms. Smith under the correct standard for voter misconduct. While it is also possible the State could charge Ms. Smith with perjury charges as it has her husband, Michael Pese, and other American Samoan defendants, the Court of Appeals questioned in a footnote whether the State could do so. Without deciding the question, it observed that “the State could potentially charge Smith with both first-degree voter misconduct and perjury, notwithstanding the fact that the legislature has chosen to enact a specialized voter misconduct statute.”

In the remaining criminal cases, the Alaska superior court is also considering motions to dismiss the charges based on the constitutional defense that Mr. Pese and others born in American Samoa - a U.S. territory for 125 years – are U.S. citizens based on the Citizenship Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. Briefing on those motions will be complete later this month.

Local News

Tupe Smith

item.title: Local ‘Morning Man’ featured in TV ad for the Pro Football Hall of Fame
item.description:
Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — NFL Network viewers in American Samoa may recognize 93KHJ Morning Man John Raynar’s voice that is featured in a TV Commercial for the Pro Football Hall of Fame. 

In the nationally televised campaign, Raynar is heard as the narrator throughout which also features 2 Time Super Bowl MVP and Steeler Hall Of Famer Lynn Swann.  

John is the long time morning show host at South Seas Broadcasting, who also runs a VoiceOver business with his wife Alice that focuses on targeting off island clients, some of which include the National Hockey League, The History Channel, Brad Pitt and character work for various video games.  

On being featured this season on the NFL Network, John Said: “It is a great honor to work on a platform that’s shared by other sons of American Samoa, Vi’i Le Atua”

Local News

item.title: Roasted Shrimp with Okra and Tomatoes
item.description:
In the South, okra and tomatoes are the crown jewels of the summer. Frying is the most common preparation for okra, but roasting also brings the best out of these two favorites; tomatoes become sweeter, and okra softens, developing a deeper savoriness brought forward by a simple seasoning of salt and pepper. Shrimp brings the dish to a new level: The smoked paprika and oregano are a perfect foil to the shrimp’s own natural, delicate flavor, and, swirled together with the olive oil and tomato juice in the pan, the result is a meal with the makings of a stew with a fraction of the time and effort. It truly tastes like a warm, summer Sunday evening. When choosing okra, go for the smaller to medium-size pods. The bigger the okra, the more likely it is to be stringy and tough. Serve with cooked rice or atop angel hair pasta.

The post Roasted Shrimp with Okra and Tomatoes appeared first on Hawaii Tribune-Herald.

item.title: Obituaries for September 6
item.description:
Nelson Levi Ahia, 79, of Hilo, died Aug. 11 at Hilo Benioff Medical Center. Born in Olaa, he was a retired relay technician for Hawaii Electric Light Co., U.S. Army Vietnam War veteran and member of Church of the Holy Apostles. Visitation 9-10 a.m. Monday, Sep. 14, at Church of the Holy Apostles Episcopal Church, 1407 Kapiolani St. in Hilo. Funeral Mass at 10 a.m. Burial to follow at Hawaii Veterans Cemetery No. 2. Aloha attire; no flowers. Survived by wife, Cindy Ahia; son, Dr. Chad Ahia; daughter, Jackie (Casey Morris) Ahia; siblings, James “Kimo” (Kathleen) Ahia Jr., Carol (Albert) Fajardo and Albert “Kalae” (Judy) Ahia; two grandchildren; nieces, nephews and cousins. Arrangements by Dodo Mortuary.

The post Obituaries for September 6 appeared first on Hawaii Tribune-Herald.

item.title: Board of Higher Education names next ASCC President
item.description:
By 
Samoa News staff
reporters@samoanews.com

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — The American Samoa Community College Board of Higher Education has chosen a new ASCC president, replacing Interim President Sonny J. Leomiti, who had taken the position vacated by former President Dr. Rosevonne Makaiwi-Pato when her contract was not renewed by the Board this year.

In a memorandum, dated September 2, 2026, the BHE Chairperson Dr. Oreta Mapu Crichton announced to ASCC Faculty, Staff, and Students that the new ASCC President is Ti’alemasunu Tupuola Dr. Mikaele Etuale, effective Sept. 8, 2026.

Dr. Crichton expressed a special note of thanks to Interim President Leomiti for his leadership during the past months, as well as to the faculty, staff, and students for their patience, resilience, and dedication through “this period of institutional transition”.

She noted that the newly chosen ASCC president brings an outstanding track record in education and public leadership across American Samoa; and, shared the following message from the incoming president to the ASCC community:

“Saili le Atamai — To Seek Knowledge. I am incredibly honored to return to the American Samoa Community College as its President. I look forward to collaborating closely with the Board, our talented faculty, dedicated staff, and inspiring students to build upon our legacy of academic excellence and service to our territory.”

The BHE chairperson concluded her announcement with a request to “please join us in giving a warm welcome to Ti’alemasunu Tupuola Dr. Mikaele Etuale and his family as we begin this exciting next chapter together.”

BACKGROUND

It was in April this year that the BHE formally notified then ASCC president Dr. Makaiwi-Pato, who had served as the President of ASCC for nearly 26 years, in a formal letter, signed by all eight members of the Board, that, “after careful consideration, the Board has determined that it will deny your contract renewal request.”  

The letter acknowledged her extensive contributions over her long tenure, noting, “We recognize and sincerely appreciate your 25 years and 9 months of leadership and service to the college.” 

However, it also highlighted that, following recent changes in Board membership, the Board is working to establish a clear strategic direction and shared priorities for the institution's future. 

Dr. Makaiwi-Pato addressed ASCC faculty and staff in a heartfelt thank-you and farewell email sent out on the following Monday. 

In her message, she expressed sincere gratitude for their efforts in organizing a well-planned and executed graduation ceremony the previous Friday, highlighting their vital role in preparing graduates for both further education and successful entry into the workforce. 

In her email, she also conveyed her appreciation for their unwavering support and belief in her leadership throughout her time as ASCC president.

Dr. Makaiwi-Pato also shared an important update regarding her contract status, indicating she received a notice of non-renewal effective May 18, and attached the Board's letter for transparency. 

“In all professional transparency, I share this with you as the Board works toward recruitment of a new President. This comes with mixed emotions – a sadness at leaving an institution where we have worked toward our mission as a family of educators, friends, and colleagues, and at this chapter now coming to an end in my leadership. Yet I leave with a joy that I have been blessed so abundantly to have worked with professionals and dedicated, committed, and talented individuals who have left their mark in my heart.” 

In closing, Dr. Makaiwi-Pato urged her colleagues to support the BHE in its upcoming search for a new President who will lead ASCC to even greater heights. She also encouraged faculty and staff to consider taking on leadership roles themselves, emphasizing the importance of continuity and a shared vision for the college's future.

ASCC President

item.title: Obituaries for September 3
item.description:
Yukie Inaba, 98, of Holualoa died March 26 at Kona Community Hospital. Born on Kauai, she was a junior accountant and member of Daifukuji Soto Mission and Waiaha Kumiai. Private services held; no flowers or koden (monetary gifts). Survived by sons, Brian (Dawn) Inaba and Derek (Renee) Inaba of Kona; daughters, Roxanne (Stan) Sanehira of Hilo and Gail (Matt) Miyasato of Seattle; seven grandchildren and a great-grandson. Arrangements by Dodo Mortuary.

item.title: Funkfit American Samoa claims a First at the 11th Annual Toa Games — in the Scaled Division
item.description:
APIA, SAMOA — Funkfit American Samoa celebrated a historic achievement after claiming first place in the Scaled Division at the 11th Annual Toa Games, a CrossFit-inspired competition hosted by CrossFit Fatu Toa in Apia, Samoa.

Competing against 12 teams, Funkfit delivered a strong and consistent performance throughout the competition to secure a top spot.

The winning team was led by Team Captain Kennedy Nofoagatotoa, alongside teammates Jarret Sunia, Olivia Hogarth, and Alzy Mailei. Together, the four athletes demonstrated strength, endurance, teamwork and determination across the competition’s challenging events.

The victory marks a monumental moment for Funkfit American Samoa, representing the gym’s first Toa Games win in any division.

The team extended special acknowledgement to Coach Claude Young of Funkfit and Walterlee Imo of CrossFit Apia for their leadership, coaching and continued commitment to preparing the athletes leading up to the Toa Games.

Funkfit also thanked their families, friends and the wider community for the tremendous love, encouragement and support they received throughout their journey.

item.title: European Union Naval Force Intercepts Suspected Russian Shadow Fleet Tanker
item.description: Italian Navy multi-purpose combat ship ITS Thaon di Revel (P430), flagship of EU Naval Force Mediterranean Irini, intercepted a Cameroon-flagged oil tanker suspected of being part of Russia’s shadow fleet on Sunday while operating in the Mediterranean. Forces from Thaon di Revel boarded MV Sun (IMO: 9293117) to verify the tanker’s flag. Sun is suspected to be part of Russia’s shadow fleet of merchant vessels and tankers used for sanction evasion. EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Kaja Kallas announced the interception in a social media post on Monday. Kallas did not disclose where the boarding took

Apia, SAMOA – 01 September 2026 – Cabinet last week approved overseas treatment for 18 patients at a cost of approximately $800,000 tala. Of the 18 patients, 11 will receive medical treatment in Fiji, six in India and one in New Zealand. The Government has allocated $12m annually for the Overseas Medical Treatment Programme.

item.title: Obituaries for September 1
item.description:
Kaliko‘onalani Chandler Gancinia, 2, of Keaau died Aug. 20 at Kaiser Permanente Moanalua Medical Center in Honolulu. Born in Hilo, she was a member of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints Waikahe 2nd Ward. Visitation 10-11:30 a.m. Saturday (Sep. 5) at The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints Hilo Stake Center, 1373 Kilauea Ave. Funeral service at noon. Burial to follow at Alae Cemetery church section. Survived by parents, Andrew and Crystal Gancinia; siblings, Kaumuali‘i Gancinia, Po‘okela Gancinia, Lanakila Gancinia, Kulia Gancinia, Kaleikaumaka Gancinia, Kapena Gancinia and Manokalanipo Gancinia; grandparents, Augusto and Cecilia Gancinia, Lloyd and Nan Chandler; great-grandmother, Mildred Kwak. Arrangements by Dodo Mortuary.

The post Obituaries for September 1 appeared first on Hawaii Tribune-Herald.

item.title: After spate of fires Search & Rescue urges residents to take proactive measures
item.description:
Currently investigations have determined these incidents are isolated
By 
Samoa News staff
reporters@samoanews.com

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — The Department of Search and Rescue (DSAR) issued an urgent statement after two major fires last week in the Nuʻuuli area — one at a residential family home and another at a commercial building. 

In their announcement, DSAR- Fire Department highlighted a concerning trend within the community: an increase in fires affecting not only homes but also businesses and surrounding brush areas. While thorough investigations have determined these incidents are isolated and not linked to one another, both the DSAR and its Fire Division take this trend seriously and emphasize the need for community vigilance.

To enhance safety, the DSAR- Fire Department is urging every resident and business owner to take proactive measures. They recommend that individuals closely supervise cooking areas to prevent accidents, stay alert for unusual odors or signs of smoke, and unplug appliances when not in use. Additionally, residents are encouraged to test their smoke alarms monthly and ensure all family members know a clear, unobstructed exit route in an emergency. 

For business owners, recommendations include keeping emergency exits clear and avoiding overloaded electrical circuits, which can pose a fire hazard. Also, remove dry brush and dead leaves from around building perimeters to prevent fires from spreading.

Last Wednesday night, a fire erupted around 10:30 PM in the Lions Park area on Lima Street, becoming the latest incident in a troubling series of approximately two dozen fires reported across American Samoa over the last three months. The fire began within a small, three-building compound situated adjacent to an ASTCA tower and communications building. Eyewitnesses at the park's ball courts, alarmed by the flames, quickly rushed over to assess the situation and determine whether anyone needed assistance.

Witnesses reported that the blaze's intense heat ignited not only a building and a nearby gazebo, but also nearby palm trees. 

In addition to the tireless efforts of first responders, ASTCA employees joined the effort to safeguard nearby communications equipment from potential damage. Workers from Samoa Motors also arrived promptly to help relocate vehicles parked in their lot across the street, ensuring emergency vehicles had unencumbered access.

Then, on Friday morning, tragedy struck again when a house fire broke out in Nuʻuuli, located behind the pool hall next to Alora’s restaurant. The incident sent one person to the hospital, making it the fourth major fire in American Samoa this month.

Neighbors reported that the house was occupied when the fire ignited around 7:30 am. Photographs posted to facebook taken at the scene showed the residence fully engulfed in smoke, with flames licking through cracks in the roof.

One eyewitness recounted the dramatic scene, noting that one person was successfully removed from the burning home and subsequently taken away by ambulance for medical care. Emergency responders extinguished the fire within about two hours, working diligently to prevent further damage. Firefighters later confirmed that the fire was linked to a vehicle parked near the house, underscoring the need for public awareness about fire safety.

This statement and the subsequent incidents underscore the heightened fire risks the community faces and the importance of preventive actions to protect lives and property.

Local News
Tags: 
fires

item.title: Steves: St. Andrews: Hit the links, books and beach
item.description:

item.description: Transits through the Strait of Hormuz rose more than 30 percent last week, with the increase mostly led by tankers and gas carriers. There were 114 transits between Aug. 17 and Sunday compared to Aug. 10-16, according to Lloyd’s List Intelligence. Those numbers are likely to fluctuate as more dark transits are confirmed. There were at least 42 westbound transits into the strait from Aug. 17 to Sunday, with 29 the week prior, according to Lloyd’s data. item.title: States, voting rights groups renew challenges to Trump plans to restrict mail-in voting
item.description:
Democratic-led states and voting rights groups on Wednesday renewed their efforts to block the U.S. Postal Service from imposing new requirements for mail-in voting before ballots go out for the November congressional elections, as ordered by President Donald Trump. Democratic attorneys general from 23 states and the District of Columbia, along with Pennsylvania’s governor, filed a newlawsuit in Boston federal court two days after the U.S. Supreme Court lifted an earlier injunction they had won blocking Trump’s order on the grounds that they sued too soon.

item.title: US inflation remains elevated as GDP growth outlook brightens
item.description:
Annual U.S. inflation held steady in July well above the Federal Reserve’s 2% target for the 65th straight month, and the unexpected pause in the decline from a recent war-induced peak is likely to intensify the central bank’s debate over whether interest rates should be lifted or held steady.

The post US inflation remains elevated as GDP growth outlook brightens appeared first on Hawaii Tribune-Herald.

item.title: American Samoa’s Latter-day Saints temple dedication, open house dates planned
item.description:
By 
Joel Randall, Church News reporter
Source: Deseret Church News

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — The Pago Pago American Samoa Temple was first announced in 1977. Now half a century later, it’s nearly complete.

Elder Quentin L. Cook of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles will dedicate the Pago Pago American Samoa Temple  on Sunday, Dec. 13.

The dedication — broadcast to all congregations in the temple district — will follow a public open house from Wednesday, Nov. 4, to Saturday, Nov. 21, excluding Sundays.

A media day will be held Nov. 2, and invited guests will tour the temple Nov. 3.

These dates were published Monday, Aug. 24, on ChurchofJesusChrist.org.

It’ll be the first temple dedicated in the United States territory of American Samoa. With dedication dates as currently announced by the Church, this would be the final temple dedicated in 2026.

ABOUT THE PAGO PAGO TEMPLE

Ground was broken for the Pago Pago temple on Oct. 30, 2021. Elder K. Brett Nattress, a General Authority Seventy and then first counselor in the Church’s Pacific Area presidency, presided over the ceremony.

“As we symbolically turn the soil,” he said, “let us turn our hearts to our Lord and Savior, Jesus Christ. Let us establish a firm foundation in our Savior.”

The Pago Pago temple plans call for a single-story, 17,000-square-foot building, located in Tafuna, American Samoa, along with housing for the temple president and missionaries and a distribution center.

THE CHURCH IN AMERICAN SAMOA

Missionary work began in present-day American Samoa in June 1888, with the opening of the Samoan Mission. Before American Samoa became a U.S. territory in 1900, the first meetinghouse constructed in Samoa was dedicated Oct. 28, 1888, in Aunu‘u. A branch was organized the same day.

On June 15, 1969, the Pago Pago Stake — the first in American Samoa — was created. From 1985 to 1991, Church membership doubled from about 5,500 members to around 11,000.

Today, American Samoa is home to more than 17,600 Latter-day Saints, meeting across 44 wards and branches.

Local News
Tags:

item.title: NOAA Ocean Exploration: Where We’ve Been, Where We’re Going
item.description:
Source: NOAA Ocean Exploration

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — On Thursday, August 20, NOAA Ship Okeanos Explorer left Rarotonga in the Cook Islands to begin a 29-day expedition to map and explore deep waters in and around American Samoa. During the expedition, the mission team will conduct remotely operated vehicle, or ROV, dives to explore the seafloor and water column and overnight mapping operations, and continuous shore-side participation via telepresence technology.

We expect to explore abyssal plain environments, with a focus on developing a baseline assessment of marine critical minerals, specifically polymetallic nodules, as well as seamount habitats, deep-sea coral and sponge communities, fish habitats, and the water column.Thanks to telepresence technology, NOAA Ocean Exploration invites anyone with an internet connection to watch and listen as members of the science community actively engage and guide each dive.

Today, August 24, the team will conduct the first dive of the expedition on a seamount near the boundary between American Samoa and the Cook Islands. They expect to launch the ROV at approximately 8:30 a.m. SST (3:30 p.m. EDT) and descend nearly 2,400 meters (1.5 miles) below the surface, to reveal the geology and marine life of this underwater mountain.

Barring any weather or technical issues, dives will be conducted daily August 24-September 1 and September 2-September 12. Most days, we expect to deploy the ROV at approximately 8 a.m. SST (3 p.m. EDT), but we’ll share updates if things change.

Join us live at oceanexplorer.noaa.gov!

This week’s tentative 2026 American Samoa ROV + Mapping expedition schedule
NOTE: All dates, times, and locations are subject to change

August 24: Dive 01 (8:30 a.m. to 8:30 p.m. SST): Seamount Dive
August 25: Dive 02 (8 a.m. to 8 p.m. SST): Abyssal Plain Dive
August 26: Dive 03 (8 a.m. to 8 p.m. SST): Abyssal Plain Dive
August 27: Dive 04 (8 a.m. to 8 p.m. SST): Abyssal Plain Dive
August 28: Dive 05 (8 a.m. to 8 p.m. SST): Abyssal Plain Dive
August 29: Dive 06 (8 a.m. to 8 p.m. SST): Abyssal Plain Dive
August 30: Dive 07 (8 a.m. to 8 p.m. SST): Abyssal Plain Dive

 

Section: 
Local News
Tags: 
NOAA Ocean Exploration

item.title: Obituaries for August 25
item.description:
Filomena Longboy Badua, 82, of Kapaau died Aug. 3 at home. Born in San Nicolas, Ilocos Norte, Philippines, she was retired from Mauna Kea Beach Hotel and a member of St. Augustine’s Episcopal Church and Kohala Filipino Community Club. Visitation with all-night vigil 6 p.m. Friday, Sep. 18 at the family home on Maulili Road. Visitation again 9-10 a.m. Saturday, Sep. 19 at St. Augustine’s Episcopal Church. Funeral Mass at 10 a.m. Burial at Hawi County Cemetery. Lunch to follow. Casual attire. Survived by sons, Bernie Badua, Edison (Sunshine) Badua of Kauai and Dennis (Florence) Pascua; daughters, Evelyn (Melvyn Ventura) Macalma and Mary Jane (Wilfred Jr.) Sulliban; brother Agustin Longboy; 14 grandchildren; and 13 great-grandchildren. Arrangements by Dodo Mortuary.

The post Obituaries for August 25 appeared first on Hawaii Tribune-Herald.

item.description:

item.title: SOUTHCOM Strikes First Suspected Drug Boat in Two Months
item.description: Forces with Joint Task Force Western Hemisphere – the new name for Joint Task Force Southern Spear – struck a low-profile vessel suspected of smuggling illicit narcotics on Sunday. The strike killed two people, according to a Monday announcement from U.S. Southern Command. In total, 223 people have been killed in strikes on vessels suspected of carrying illicit drugs. The Sunday strike in the Eastern Pacific is the first one in over two months. Gen. Francis Donovan, commander of SOUTHCOM, ordered the strike. “Confirmed intelligence revealed the vessel’s active involvement in narco-trafficking,” reads the SOUTHCOM post on social media site

item.title: ASCC expresses condolences at the passing of Cherylmoanamarie Ripley
item.description:
By 
ASCC Staff

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA —  The American Samoa Community College has joined the family and friends of Ms. Cherylmoanamarie “Cherie” Ripley in mourning her passing earlier this month. Until her retirement in 2024, Ms. Ripley contributed decades of service to the College, and was recognized by many as one of the pillars of its day-to-day operations. She was by far the most experienced of the College’s administrative staff, and is remembered for her in-depth knowledge and congenial personality.

Ms. Ripley’s tenure with ASCC dates all the way back to 1977, when she took the position of Secretary to the President. After three years with the Office of the President, Ms. Ripley transitioned to another secretarial role with the Instructional Support Division, under which she also served as an Administrative Assistant and Computer Lab monitor. In 1985 she joined the College’s Adult Education Department, once again as an Administrative Assistant, a title she took with her in her next transition to the Office of the Dean of Instruction in 1997. In 2003, Ms. Ripley joined the Institutional Affairs Division as its Website Administrator, serving until she became Special Assistant to the Dean of Academic Affairs four years later. Ms. Ripley remained with the Division of Academic Affairs until her retirement in 2024.

ASCC Dean of Academic Affairs Dr. Siamaua Ropeti, with whom Ms. Ripley spent her final years at the College, still expresses appreciation for her expertise. “As my special assistant”, recalled Dean Ropeti, “Cherie faithfully executed her role in all capacities, encompassing responsibilities such as initiating contracts, submitting time sheets and memos on behalf of the Division, doing waivers, assisting with graduation, preparation for Orientation and so much more.  

“Even after she retired, she continued to visit ASCC and mingle with her friends and colleagues until she was no longer able to do so. We still feel her presence, and take inspiration from her selfless dedication, her tautua to any fa'alavelave involving ASCC employees, and her commitment to order, instruction and quality service.

“To people who knew her, she was the epitome of professionalism. Our office considered her the elder sister, the advisor, and the glue that held the Division of Academic Affairs Office together. She will never be forgotten.”

Looking back on her decades with ASCC, as she prepared to retire, Ms. Ripley wrote in a 2024 letter to then-President Dr. Rosevonne Makaiwi-Pato, “I will be tossing in the towel from my post as ASCC Special Administrative Assistant to the Dean of Academic Affairs.  I will be leaving the Halls of Ivy of the American Samoa Community College after almost 50 years of dedication and returning to Sogi, Leone, Fofo County to focus wholeheartedly on my Ripley family, my village of Leone functions, and Siona Le Mauga Pa’ia Congregational Christian Church of Leone until I am called home to serve our Heavenly Father.”

Ms. Ripley received that call in August 2026, bringing full circle a career during which she played a vital supporting role in the evolution of ASCC. 

The administration, faculty and staff of the College offer their most sincere condolences to the Ripley family, and in the words of Interim President Sonny J. Leomiti, “Those of us who knew Cherie, and that is practically all of us, will always remember her with great fondness.”  

[Editor’s Note: Samoa News offers its sincere condolences to Cherie’s family at her passing. She was a friend from days we all began by respecting the journey we each chose to take, the road traveled. While, we did not always stay in contact, whenever met, we greeted each other with a smile full of grace, acknowledging respect for our choices. Manuia lou malaga Cherie — may God’s blessings be yours.]

Local News

Cherie

item.title: 2 Mariners Killed in Strait of Hormuz as Transits See Small Increase
item.description: Two mariners were killed in the past week and a half in the Strait of Hormuz by Iranian attacks. On Monday, an Iranian attack on MV Minoan Dignity in the strait left one seafarer dead. It is the second attack on a ship managed by Greek company Modion Maritime Management. On Aug. 3, MV Minoan Pioneer was struck, with the International Maritime Organization reporting one missing seafarer. It is not clear if the seafarer has been recovered. Two days before the attack on Minoan Dignity, Iran also hit MV Riyan Star in the Strait of Hormuz, killing one crew member.

item.title: Amata highlights Congressional reforms to Medicaid, appreciates CMS Visit
item.description:
Source: Congresswoman Uifa’atali Amata’s D.C. staff

Washington, D.C. — Congresswoman Uifa’atali Amata’s District Office staff, led by her District Director, Dr. Uta Laloulu Tagoilelagi, met earlier this month with officials from the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS), to discuss Medicaid services, travel, needs and priorities.

“In recent years, in Congress, we have increased our highest possible availability of Medicaid federal dollars for American Samoa by about ten times the amount it was 12 years ago, and boosted our FMAP from 55 to 83 percent, the highest rate in the nation,” Congresswoman Amata said. “While Congress has improved the big picture, I’m always concerned that the results reach the people who need it most. I appreciate the ongoing work of CMS and ASG to strengthen services and care for our people, but health care challenges here are a constant priority due to our geography and population size,” she continued.

“Thank you to CMS for sending officials to our islands, their willingness to discuss services, and I ask them to continue to look for any and all support they can facilitate for our people. They had a productive discussion in my office, as well as their meeting with ASG officials and Governor Pulaali’i.”

Congressional Medicaid Improvements for American Samoa

    •    Historic reform: Congress passed major bipartisan Medicaid reforms and improvements for American Samoa in 2019, with the support of Congresswoman Amata and other territory representatives.
    •    Ten-fold Increase: This sweeping change went into effect in 2020 and greatly expanded American Samoa’s total available federal funds under the ceiling from $12 million in fiscal year 2019 to over $80 million the very next year, plus yearly increases since indexed to medical inflation rates, currently estimated at $88-90 million – approximately an increase by ten times the amount since fy2015.
    •    83% Match: Under that bipartisan legislation, Congress raised American Samoa’s standard Medicaid federal match (FMAP) to 83 percent under federal statute, up from just 55 percent where it had been for many years.
    •    Long-term Change: Then in 2022, Congress followed up with another major improvement (Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2023), again with the bipartisan support of Amata and all the territory’s representatives, making American Samoa’s standard 83 percent FMAP rate permanent, no longer at risk of reverting back to 55 percent. This breakthrough means it no longer must be passed over again every few years.
    •    Nation’s Best Rate: American Samoa’s standard federal match (FMAP) is now secure and the highest in the nation – at a better rate than any of the 50 states. The only time the rate can be higher is under a major disaster scenario such as after Storm Gita or during Covid’s peak.
    •    Next effort: Finally, in ongoing work, Amata is an original cosponsor of the bipartisan Medicaid Improvement for Insular Areas Act, H.R. 3154, working together as territories toward removing the Medicaid ceiling entirely, a forward-thinking goal so that American Samoa’s ceiling could never become a future problem. American Samoa’s Medicaid program began in 1983 under a federal funding cap that does not apply to states in the same way, so it is also a matter of principle, to bring about parity with the states on this remaining reform.

Local News
Tags: 
Congresswoman Uifa’atali Amata

item.title: Taiwan extends entry limits for DRC residents over Ebola
item.description: Taipei, Aug. 21 (CNA) Taiwan will extend entry restrictions on residents of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) for another 90 days until Nov. 28, with limited exceptions, to reduce the risk of Ebola being imported into the country, the Taiwan Centers for Disease Control (CDC) said Friday.
item.source:markdown: Taipei, Aug. 21 (CNA) Taiwan will extend entry restrictions on residents of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) for another 90 days until Nov. 28, with limited exceptions, to reduce the risk of Ebola being imported into the country, the Taiwan Centers for Disease Control (CDC) said Friday.

item.title: Heavy rain forecast for southern Taiwan through Monday
item.description: Taipei, Aug. 21 (CNA) The Central Weather Administration (CWA) said Friday that southwesterly winds and a low‑pressure system will bring heavy to torrential rain to southern Taiwan through Monday, while other regions can expect afternoon downpours.

item.title: Conservation plans formed for 3 endangered native Taiwanese plants
item.description: Taipei, Aug. 21 (CNA) Conservation action plans for three endangered plant species native to Taiwan have been jointly developed by the Taiwan Biodiversity Research Institute (TBRI) and the Forestry and Nature Conservation Agency (FANCA), the Ministry of Agriculture said Friday.

item.title: Opposition fast‑tracks condemnation motion against premier
item.description: Taipei, Aug. 21 (CNA) Opposition lawmakers voted Friday to fast-track a motion condemning Premier Cho Jung-tai (卓榮泰) following his refusal to countersign a youth savings legislation recently passed by the Legislature, alongside other bills.

item.title: Asian children's literature event opens in Tainan with sustainability focus
item.description: Taipei, Aug. 21 (CNA) Around 150 children's literature professionals from across the Asia-Pacific region gathered in Tainan, southern Taiwan, on Friday for a three-day convention exploring how books and reading can promote sustainability and global citizenship.

item.title: 'Chainsmoker Cat' anime series violates tobacco rules: Health minister
item.description: Taipei, Aug. 21 (CNA) Health Minister Shih Chung-liang (石崇良) said Friday that the Japanese anime series "Chainsmoker Cat" (尼古喵喵) contains scenes that violate Taiwan's tobacco control rules, including close-ups of cigarette brands and smoking scenes without health warnings.

item.title: Obituaries for August 21
item.description:
Delbert Chang, 89, of Papaikou died July 24 at Hilo Benioff Medical Center. Born in Waipi‘o Valley, he was a retired butcher for Safeway, a salesman for the former Miko Meats. A 2006 inductee into the big Island Sports Hall of Fame, he was a 156-pound Big Island and territorial champion boxer in the 1950s, and was a longtime volunteer coach for the Wanderers Athletic Club, Papaikou Hongwanji Club, Papaikou Cougars Pop Warner Football and the Big Island Amateur Boxing Association. Visitation 4-6 p.m. Friday (Aug. 28) at Dodo Mortuary Chapel. Funeral service at 6 p.m. Graveside committal service 10 a.m. Saturday, Aug. 29, at Homelani Memorial Park, Ilima Section. Casual attire. Survived by daughters, Sheila (Keith) Ogawa and Sharon (Don) Hirota of Hilo, Sandi (Darren) Rosario of Papaikou; brothers, Gilbert (Okyo) Chang and Jerry Chang of Hilo; sister, Shirlene (Leroy) Rayoan of Hilo; sisters-in-law, Promise Grace and Ruth Takayama of Hilo; nine grandchildren and seven great-grandchildren; nieces, nephews and cousins. Arrangements by Dodo Mortuary.

The post Obituaries for August 21 appeared first on Hawaii Tribune-Herald.
